performers: Soojin Han, violin; Hankyung Arte Philharmonic; Seokwon Hong, conductor
intro: A quiet E-minor link leads to the trumpet calls and flying violin notes of Mendelssohn’s finale. Soojin Han and the Hankyung Arte Philharmonic finish the concerto in E major, with the soloist still running when the last chords arrive.

sections.label: Link · Solo violin and strings in E minor
sections.mNote: Allegretto non troppo: fourteen bars between song and dance

sections.label: Link · The strings settle on B
sections.mNote: A swell, a diminuendo and a held pause

sections.label: A · Trumpet calls and flying violin notes
sections.mNote: Allegro molto vivace launches the E-major finale

sections.label: B · A short violin tune in B major
sections.mNote: The solo melody opens into rising and falling arpeggios

sections.label: Dev · The tune turns towards G major
sections.mNote: The orchestra’s version leads into a short development

sections.label: A′ · The violin returns with string replies
sections.mNote: The strings add a second melody around the soloist

cues.title: Fourteen bars between movements
cues.text: The solo violin and strings make a short bridge out of the Andante. Fourteen bars, in E minor, marked Allegretto non troppo. The winds and brass wait while the violin sings one more measured phrase.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Rietz edition, plate M.B. 18, p. 37, Allegretto non troppo. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/a/af/IMSLP24558-PMLP04931-Mendelssohn_Violin_Concerto_Op.64.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Trumpets open the door
cues.text: Two clipped fanfares from bassoons, horns, trumpets and timpani start the Allegro molto vivace. Between them, the violin darts upward. Soon the strings join its quick E-major tune, keeping their bows light.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Rietz edition, pp. 37–38: opening fanfares, solo entry and light string accompaniment.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Fairy music
cues.text: Steven Ledbetter calls this finale one of those brilliantly light and fleet-footed examples of “fairy music” that Mendelssohn made so uniquely his own. The strings keep their bows light beneath the soloist’s flying notes.
cues.evidence: Steven Ledbetter, Boston Symphony Orchestra programme note, on the finale as “fairy music”: https://www.bso.org/works/mendelssohn-violin-concerto Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Rietz edition, pp. 38–41, for the light string accompaniment under the solo violin: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/a/af/IMSLP24558-PMLP04931-Mendelssohn_Violin_Concerto_Op.64.pdf

cues.title: A short tune in B
cues.text: The solo violin has a second tune, brief and light, in B major. It soon opens into arpeggios that climb and fall across the strings. The orchestra keeps answering in short phrases, leaving the soloist plenty of room to move.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Rietz edition, pp. 40–42. The B-major second theme and following arpeggios are described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Violin_Concerto_(Mendelssohn).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The orchestra borrows the tune
cues.text: The orchestra plays its own version of the opening tune, then the development turns towards G major. The violin keeps up its quick notes while short wind phrases appear around it. This is a compact detour; the finale is soon on its way back.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Rietz edition, pp. 42–45. The orchestral variation and G-major development are described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Violin_Concerto_(Mendelssohn).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The strings have another tune
cues.text: The opening tune returns to the solo violin, with a new melody answering it in the strings. Mendelssohn marks the quiet playing carefully: sempre pp, always pianissimo. The violin’s little leaps and runs have company now.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Rietz edition, pp. 46–48: solo theme, string countermelody and sempre pp. The added countermelody is also described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Violin_Concerto_(Mendelssohn).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Mendelssohn takes the baton
cues.text: On 23 October 1845 Mendelssohn conducts the Gewandhaus’s third concert of the season, and Ferdinand David plays the concerto there for the second time. Mendelssohn had led none of the previous winter’s concerts, the première included. David has helped shape the solo part through years of letters and advice.
cues.evidence: Alfred Dörffel, Geschichte der Gewandhausconcerte zu Leipzig (1884), p. 111: Mendelssohn conducted part of the 1845–46 concerts and led Schumann’s B♭ symphony in the third concert, on 23 October; the same evening David played Mendelssohn’s violin concerto “zum zweiten Male”. Pp. 109–110: Mendelssohn conducted none of the 1844–45 concerts (Internet Archive, geschichtederge00konzgoog). Steven Ledbetter describes David’s advice and correspondence: https://www.bso.org/works/mendelssohn-violin-concerto

cues.title: Trills under the woodwinds
cues.text: The violin settles into long trills while the woodwinds recall the main tune. Plucked strings mark the pulse underneath. After so much racing about, the soloist stays on one spot and lets the tune pass overhead.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Rietz edition, p. 52: sustained solo trills, woodwind melody and pizzicato strings.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The last sprint in E
cues.text: The trills open into more running notes, and the coda drives towards E major. The orchestra answers the violin’s scales with sharply accented chords. A final upward rush brings the soloist and orchestra together for the closing chords.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Rietz edition, pp. 53–55: final solo runs, orchestral accents and E-major close.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The strings wait on B
transitions.from: Link · Solo violin and strings in E minor
transitions.to: Link · The strings settle on B
transitions.how: The E-minor link swells with the solo violin and strings alone. Its bass settles on B, the dominant of E, as the strings diminish to pianissimo. The violin holds above it, and a fermata suspends the last chord.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Rietz edition, p. 37, final bars of the Allegretto non troppo.

transitions.title: A fanfare breaks the pause
transitions.from: Link · The strings settle on B
transitions.to: A · Trumpet calls and flying violin notes
transitions.how: After the fermata, bassoons, horns, trumpets and timpani strike a fanfare at fortissimo. The marking changes to Allegro molto vivace. The solo violin answers with a rising figure; the strings join as the E-major main tune gets under way.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Rietz edition, pp. 37–38: held dominant, fanfares and beginning of the fast solo theme.

transitions.title: The violin finds a B-major tune
transitions.from: A · Trumpet calls and flying violin notes
transitions.to: B · A short violin tune in B major
transitions.how: The violin’s rising runs and an orchestral chord lead into B major, the dominant key. The soloist begins a quieter phrase, marked leggiero, over short string chords and plucked basses. Woodwinds answer between its quick notes.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Rietz edition, pp. 40–41: ascent into the B-major second theme, leggiero marking and accompaniment.

transitions.title: The orchestra takes a turn
transitions.from: B · A short violin tune in B major
transitions.to: Dev · The tune turns towards G major
transitions.how: The solo violin finishes its B-major arpeggios with another upward scale. The orchestra answers with a fortissimo version of the opening tune. As the violin rejoins, the music turns towards G major for a short development, with light string chords beneath its runs.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Rietz edition, pp. 42–44. The G-major development after the orchestral variation is described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Violin_Concerto_(Mendelssohn).

transitions.title: The returning violin gains a partner
transitions.from: Dev · The tune turns towards G major
transitions.to: A′ · The violin returns with string replies
transitions.how: The quick solo runs lead back to the opening tune. Under the violin, the strings add a second melody, marked sempre pp, with plucked bass notes beneath. The return heads towards E major while the woodwinds keep their short replies.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Rietz edition, pp. 46–48: solo return and string countermelody. The recapitulation’s added melody is described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Violin_Concerto_(Mendelssohn).

transitions.title: The second tune stays in E
transitions.from: A′ · The violin returns with string replies
transitions.to: B′ · The second tune returns in E major
transitions.how: The short violin tune that first appeared in B major returns in E major. Strings keep their clipped accompaniment and the basses punctuate the phrases. The violin soon resumes its rising and falling arpeggios, with woodwind answers above.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Rietz edition, pp. 50–52. The return of the second theme in E major is described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Violin_Concerto_(Mendelssohn).

transitions.title: The trill becomes a scale
transitions.from: B′ · The second tune returns in E major
transitions.to: Coda · Scales race towards the final chords
transitions.how: Over plucked strings, the violin’s long trill accompanies the woodwind tune. It breaks into descending scales, then repeated notes as the orchestra gathers. The final E-major stretch alternates running violin figures with accented orchestral chords, ending in one last upward scale.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Rietz edition, pp. 52–55: trills, renewed solo passagework and the E-major ending.

source.title: Mendelssohn, Violin Concerto in E minor, Op. 64, full score (Leipzig: Breitkopf & Härtel; Rietz edition, Serie 4 No. 18)
source.locator: III. Allegretto non troppo — Allegro molto vivace, pp. 37–55: string link and fanfares, p. 37; orchestral theme and development, pp. 42–45; solo trills with woodwinds, p. 52; closing pages, pp. 53–55.

timeline.note: The soloist and strings play the fourteen-bar E-minor link; winds, brass and timpani wait.
Bassoons, horns, trumpets and timpani strike two short fanfares, answered by the solo violin.
The violin’s quick E-major theme runs above a light string accompaniment.
The orchestra plays its own version of the opening tune, then the soloist rejoins for the development.
Woodwinds recall the main tune above the violin’s long trills and plucked strings.
The violin races through its last scales as the full orchestra closes in E major.

fields.note: The video description on the YouTube channel named “한수진 Soojin Han” reads “Vn. Soojin Han / Cond. Seokwon Hong / Orch. Hankyung Arte Philharmonic”. The Commons file page names only the orchestra as author, linking the orchestra’s own site. That site’s news column reports a later concert (September 2026) played by the orchestra under a conductor named 홍석원 (Hong Seok-won, professor at Seoul National University), which supports the association but says nothing about the 2022 concert. No roster of players is given, and no second source for the soloist was opened.

composer.epithet: At sixteen, he made eight string players sound like the most exhilarating orchestra in Europe.
facts: Ludwig Berger, piano; Carl Friedrich Zelter, composition
Düsseldorf music director, 1833–35; Leipzig Gewandhaus conductor from 1835
Married Cécile Jeanrenaud in 1837; five children; brother of Fanny Hensel
Leipzig Conservatoire, founded 1843; ten visits to Britain
composer.background:
In 1825, sixteen-year-old Felix Mendelssohn wrote a birthday present for his violin teacher, Eduard Rietz. It required four violins, two violas and two cellos, and gave Rietz a first-violin part that climbs out over the other seven players in long, buoyant arcs. The E♭ major Octet still sounds like someone discovering how much pleasure eight string instruments can make. Eleven years later, its composer played second viola in a public performance. Writing to Karl Klingemann on 31 January 1836, he admitted to “heart palpitations”.

He had been noisy from the start. In 1812, his sister Fanny wrote to friends in Hamburg: “Felix has a strong voice and sings all day.” He was born there on 3 February 1809; the family moved to Berlin two years later. His father Abraham was a banker, his grandfather Moses the Jewish philosopher. Abraham and Lea Mendelssohn had their children baptised as Christians in 1816 and used the additional surname Bartholdy. Fanny and Felix learnt piano with Ludwig Berger and composition with Carl Friedrich Zelter.
